title: Five Myths About Teacher Professional Learning
author: Jim Knight
summary: Drawing on 25 years studying professional learning and coaching, Jim Knight identifies five myths he once believed that persist widely in schools. Myth 1, that workshops change practice, is undercut by the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve and the reality that one-size-fits-all delivery rarely survives without follow-up coaching. Myth 2, that teachers resist change, is reframed: people resist changes they don't find worthwhile or don't believe they can execute, which Knight argues should shift leaders from asking 'why are teachers resistant' to 'what am I doing that leads to teachers not implementing.' Myth 3 is that people are motivated by goals others set for them -- Knight argues real ownership requires teachers to set their own goals in partnership with leaders. Myth 4 is that coaches don't need deep understanding of the strategies they share; he counters that vague understanding produces vague, unusable checklists, and recommends building detailed 'instructional playbooks.' Myth 5 is that improvement begins with proven practices implemented 'with fidelity' -- a research-to-consultant-to-teacher-to-student pipeline Knight argues should be inverted to a student-first model, where practices are adapted until a student-focused goal is actually hit, rather than measured by rigid checklist adherence.
points: Myth 1's evidentiary backbone is the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve (50% forgotten within 24 hours, 70-80% within a week), which explains why standalone workshops without coaching follow-up rarely change classroom practice.

Myth 2 reframes 'resistance' as misalignment: Knight cites Grenny and Patterson's two-question test (is it worth it? can I do it?) as the actual predictor of whether a teacher implements a change, not some fixed trait of resistance.

Myth 4's 'instructional playbook' solution -- 15-20 high-impact strategies with one-page research summaries and implementation checklists -- gives coaches a concrete tool for surfacing whether they actually understand a strategy deeply enough to teach it.

Myth 5's inverted model (Student to Teacher to Coach to Research, rather than Research to Consultant to Teacher to Student) relocates the standard for success from checklist fidelity to whether student learning, engagement, or well-being actually changed.
quotes: Unfortunately, people rarely implement what they learn in workshops, often because they quickly forget most of what they hear.
What I have learned, however, is that people don’t resist change, per se. They only resist change they don’t feel comfortable with or don’t see the point to.
Blaming teachers for resisting is like blaming students for not learning. A better approach is to create conditions that make real change possible.

When I ask coaches and other leaders to create checklists for the strategies they share, for example, I find that they often don’t have a deep, nuanced understanding of the strategies they are sharing with teachers.
High-quality teaching should be measured by student learning and well-being, not by rigid adherence to a prescribed checklist.
The real focus should be to ensure there are powerful improvements in student learning, achievement, and well-being.
